concepts.title: Sound as a Mechanical Wave
concepts.definition: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies and travels as a mechanical wave - a sequence of compressions and rarefactions - through a material medium; it cannot travel through vacuum, and the particles of the medium only oscillate while the wave moves forward.
concepts.key_idea: Vibration to medium to ear: sound needs matter to ride on, vacuum kills it.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc110.txt sections on production and propagation of sound
question_patterns: how is sound produced - explain with an example
why does sound not travel through vacuum - justify
what are compressions and rarefactions in a sound wave
is a sound wave mechanical or electromagnetic - justify
explain how sound reaches our ears from a source
demonstrate that sound needs a medium to travel

solution_steps.explain: The source vibrates and pushes the neighbouring particles.
Compressions and rarefactions travel onward through the medium.
The eardrum vibrates with the arriving wave and we hear.

concepts.title: Characteristics of Sound Waves
concepts.definition: Three quantities describe a sound wave: frequency, the number of compressions per second heard as pitch; amplitude, the size of the oscillation heard as loudness; and wavelength with speed, which tie together as speed equals frequency times wavelength.
concepts.key_idea: Frequency sets pitch, amplitude sets loudness, and v = f times wavelength ties them.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc110.txt sections on frequency, amplitude, wavelength, pitch and loudness
question_patterns: find the speed of sound of frequency 500 Hz and wavelength 0.68 m
differentiate pitch and loudness with examples

solution_steps.explain: The wave equation gives the speed of sound.

concepts.title: Reflection of Sound: Echo and Reverberation
concepts.definition: Sound bounces off hard surfaces like light: an echo is a reflected sound heard separately when the reflecting surface lies far enough - at least 17.2 metres for a 0.1 second gap - while multiple rapid reflections inside halls pile up as reverberation, tamed by soft absorbent panels.
concepts.key_idea: Reflection distance rule: 17.2 m keeps the echo half a second behind the original.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc110.txt sections on echo, reverberation and applications
question_patterns: what is an echo - state the condition to hear it clearly
why are cinema halls given soft ceilings and curtains
find the minimum distance to hear an echo in air
define reverberation and how it is reduced
how does a bat use reflection of sound - explain
an echo returns in the given time - find the distance of the reflecting surface

solution_steps.explain: A hard distant surface returns the wave.
The echo must arrive at least 0.1 s later, needing about 17.2 m in air.
Concert halls absorb extra reflections; SONAR and bats exploit them.

concepts.title: Range of Hearing and Ultrasound Applications
concepts.definition: Human ears hear roughly 20 Hz to 20000 Hz: sounds below this range are infrasound and above it ultrasound; ultrasound's short wavelengths let it clean, weld, image the body in sonography and detect undersea objects through SONAR.
concepts.key_idea: Beyond human ears lies ultrasound - short waves that see, clean and measure.
concepts.textbook_ref: iesc110.txt sections on hearing range and ultrasound applications
question_patterns: state the audible range of frequency for humans
what is ultrasound - give two of its applications
how does SONAR measure the depth of the sea
name two animals that can hear ultrasound
what is infrasound with an example
explain sonography using ultrasound waves

solution_steps.explain: 20 Hz to 20000 Hz is audible; outside lie infra and ultrasound.
High frequencies travel as narrow beams that reflect cleanly.
Cleaning, welding, medical imaging and SONAR exploit these reflections.
